subject: physics
title: Stress, strain and the Young modulus
key_idea: Stress is force per unit cross-sectional area and strain is extension per unit original length. Their ratio, for a material obeying Hooke's law, is the Young modulus. It describes the material itself, not the size of the sample.

blocks.text: Force and extension depend on the size of the sample. Stress and strain remove that, so materials can be compared.

items.meaning: The force applied per unit cross-sectional area. It can be tensile or compressive.
The change in length per unit original length.

blocks.label: Strain
where: ΔL = change in length (extension or compression), in m

items: Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no unit. It is often written as a percentage.
A thicker wire has a larger area, so the same force gives a smaller stress.
A longer wire gives a larger extension for the same strain.
Stress = force ÷ cross-sectional area, in Pa.
Strain = extension ÷ original length, with no unit.

blocks.text: For a material that obeys Hooke's law, stress is directly proportional to strain.

diagram.alt: A slider showing a wire under tension. For a chosen metal, force and cross-sectional area, it shows the stress, the strain and the extension.

items: The Young modulus is the stress divided by the strain. It is a property of the **material**.
A material with a large Young modulus is stiff: a large stress gives only a small strain.
On a stress–strain graph, the gradient of the straight part is the Young modulus.
The units of E are the same as stress: pascals. Common metals have values of about 7 × 10¹⁰ to 2 × 10¹¹ Pa.
The same value applies to tension and compression.
Young modulus = stress ÷ strain, in Pa.
It is the gradient of the straight part of a stress–strain graph.

blocks.text: A stress–strain graph shows how a material behaves, whatever the size of the sample.

diagram.alt: Stress–strain graphs for a ductile metal, a brittle material and a polymer. The metal rises steeply, yields, peaks and breaks. The brittle material is a steep straight line that stops at fracture. The polymer is a gentle curve.

items.meaning: The maximum stress a material can withstand before it starts to break.
The stress at which the material fractures.

items: A **ductile** material, such as copper, shows a lot of plastic deformation before it breaks. It can be drawn into wires.
A **brittle** material, such as glass, fractures with almost no plastic deformation.
A **polymeric** material, such as polythene, has a low Young modulus and a curved graph, and it stretches a long way.
Strain is plotted on the horizontal axis and stress on the vertical axis.
The area under a stress–strain graph is the energy stored per unit volume.
Ductile: much plastic deformation. Brittle: breaks with almost none.
UTS is the highest stress reached. Breaking stress is the stress at fracture.

sections.heading: Finding the Young modulus of a metal wire

blocks.text: A long thin wire gives a large strain for a small force, so the extension is easy to measure.

items.text: Clamp a long wire at one end. Pass it over a pulley and hang a weight hanger on the other end. Fix a marker on the wire next to a ruler.
Measure the original length L from the clamp to the marker with a metre rule.
Measure the diameter with a micrometer at several places and take a mean. Calculate A = πd² / 4.
Add masses in equal steps. Record the extension each time, then take the readings again on unloading.
Plot stress against strain, or force against extension. Use the gradient to find E.

items: The gradient of a force–extension graph is F/ΔL, so E = gradient × L / A.
The diameter has the biggest effect on the result, because the area depends on d².
Keep the loads small enough to stay within the limit of proportionality.
Use a long, thin wire and a reference wire to allow for changes in room temperature and a sagging support.
Measure L, the diameter and the extension for different loads.
Find E from the gradient of the graph and E = gradient × L / A.

checks.q: A wire of cross-sectional area 0.50 mm² carries a tension of 80 N. Calculate the stress in the wire.
A 2.0 m wire extends by 1.0 mm. Its Young modulus is 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. Calculate the stress in the wire.
Describe how the stress–strain graph of a ductile material differs from that of a brittle material.
checks.a: A ductile material shows a large amount of plastic deformation, so the graph continues after the elastic region and reaches a maximum stress before it breaks. A brittle material gives a straight line that ends suddenly at fracture, with almost no plastic deformation.

items: Write the Young modulus as E = FL / AΔL, from tensile stress ÷ tensile strain.
Use stress–strain graphs to find the Young modulus. Take the gradient of the straight part.
One simple method of measurement is required. The wire method above is a suitable one, and it is the basis of Required practical 4.
The equations work for **tensile or compressive** stress and strain.
Be able to draw and interpret tensile or compressive stress–strain graphs.
Know the term **breaking stress**: the stress at which the material breaks.
You must be able to **define** stress, strain and the Young modulus, and to use them.
State the definitions in words: stress is force per unit cross-sectional area, strain is extension per unit original length, and the Young modulus is stress divided by strain.
Know the terms stress, strain and **ultimate tensile strength**.
Write the Young modulus as E = σ / ε.
Be able to sketch and compare stress–strain graphs for typical ductile, brittle and polymeric materials.
Know the techniques and procedures for determining the Young modulus of a metal.
